title: SQL Database Cheat Sheet

introduction.heading: SQL: Querying & Managing Relational Databases
introduction.description: A quick reference for working with relational databases (MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite, and friends) - creating tables, reading and writing data, joining across tables, aggregating results, and keeping your data consistent with constraints and transactions.

prerequisites: A relational database installed locally (MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite) or a hosted instance
A SQL client to run queries (psql, mysql CLI, TablePlus, DBeaver, or your editor's built-in client)
Basic understanding of tables, rows, and columns

steps.title: Set Up a Database (Local or Hosted)
steps.description: Before writing any SQL you need somewhere for it to run. Pick a local install for full control, or a free hosted instance to skip setup entirely.
steps.note: MySQL and SQLite work the same way in spirit - install locally, or use a hosted instance from a provider with a free tier (Neon or Supabase for PostgreSQL, Railway or Aiven for MySQL) - only the exact commands differ.

steps.title: Get Your Connection String
steps.description: Everything your app needs to reach the database - host, port, credentials, and database name - is bundled into one connection string (URI).
steps.note: Never hardcode the connection string in your code or commit it to git - store it in a .env file and add .env to .gitignore.

steps.title: Install Driver Packages
steps.description: Install the PostgreSQL driver and dotenv so your Node.js app can read the connection string and talk to the database.

subSteps.title: .env Configuration
subSteps.description: Create a .env file in your project root with the database credentials.
subSteps.note: Add .env to your .gitignore file! Create .env.example with dummy values for documentation.

steps.title: Connect from Node.js
steps.description: Open a connection pool and run a test query to confirm everything is wired up correctly.
steps.note: A Pool (rather than a single Client) reuses connections across requests, which is what you want in a real app - open one pool at startup and reuse it everywhere.

steps.title: Create a Database & Table
steps.description: Every SQL project starts with a database and at least one table. A table's columns each have a data type and, optionally, constraints.
steps.note: SERIAL (PostgreSQL) auto-increments the id. In MySQL use INT AUTO_INCREMENT; in SQLite use INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT.

steps.title: Common Data Types
steps.description: The most-used column types across MySQL/PostgreSQL/SQLite. Exact names vary slightly by engine, but the concepts map directly.
steps.note: Use DECIMAL, never FLOAT/DOUBLE, for anything involving money - floating point types round in ways that lose cents.

steps.title: Insert, Update & Delete Rows
steps.description: The three statements that change data. Always pair UPDATE and DELETE with a WHERE clause, or every row in the table is affected.
steps.note: Running UPDATE or DELETE without a WHERE clause changes/removes every row in the table. Test with a SELECT using the same WHERE first.

steps.title: SELECT & Filter with WHERE
steps.description: SELECT reads data back out. WHERE narrows it down; ORDER BY and LIMIT control the order and how many rows come back.
steps.note: LIKE 'j%' matches anything starting with 'j'; '%j' matches anything ending with 'j'; '%j%' matches anything containing 'j'.

steps.title: JOINs Across Tables
steps.description: JOINs combine rows from related tables using a shared key (typically a foreign key). INNER JOIN is the one you reach for most; the others keep rows that don't have a match.
steps.note: LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left (first) table and fills in NULLs where there's no match on the right.

steps.title: Aggregate Functions & GROUP BY
steps.description: Aggregate functions collapse many rows into a single summary value. GROUP BY runs that aggregation once per unique value in a column; HAVING filters on the aggregated result (WHERE can't, since it runs before grouping).
steps.note: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation. Trying to use an aggregate like COUNT(*) in WHERE is a common error.

steps.title: Constraints & Relationships
steps.description: Constraints tell the database to enforce rules for you, so bad data (duplicates, orphaned rows, missing required fields) never makes it into a table in the first place.
steps.note: ON DELETE CASCADE removes an order automatically when its user is deleted. Other options: SET NULL, RESTRICT (block the delete).

steps.title: Indexes for Query Performance
steps.description: An index lets the database find matching rows without scanning the whole table - essential for columns you filter, join, or sort on frequently in large tables.
steps.note: Indexes speed up reads but slow down writes (every INSERT/UPDATE has to update the index too) - add them where you actually query, not on every column.

steps.title: Transactions
steps.description: A transaction groups multiple statements so they succeed or fail together - critical whenever one logical action touches more than one table (like transferring money between two accounts).
steps.note: Without a transaction, a crash between the two UPDATEs would leave money deducted from one account and never credited to the other.

steps.title: Common Errors & Fixes
steps.description: The errors you'll hit most often when starting out, and what they actually mean.
steps.note: When in doubt, run the failing query alone (outside any transaction) to isolate exactly which statement and which part of it is wrong.
